headline: California's Rarest Frog Gets Second Chance
meta_description: 650 southern mountain yellow-legged frogs released into San Gabriel Mountains as part of major conservation effort to save critically endangered species.
summary_short: Conservation groups released 650 endangered frogs into California mountains, marking progress in a 20-year effort to save a species down to fewer than 200 in the wild.
body:
In August, conservation organizations released 650 southern mountain yellow-legged frogs into the San Gabriel Mountains—a milestone in efforts to rescue one of Southern California's most imperiled amphibians from extinction. The Aquarium of the Pacific, Los Angeles Zoo, and U.S. Geological Survey coordinated the release, with nearly 400 of those frogs bred and reared at the Aquarium since 2021. The species has collapsed dramatically from its former abundance; a 2023 survey counted fewer than 200 frogs remaining in the southern population, a decline of about 98%. Once so common that early biologists struggled to walk without stepping on them, these frogs now cling to survival through intensive captive breeding and carefully managed reintroductions.

The work begins before dawn. Staff start catching the newly metamorphosed frogs—each about an inch long and remarkably fast—around 4 a.m., packing eight to twelve individuals into containers for a two-hour drive to the release sites. After floating the containers in the mountain streams to let the frogs acclimate, the team watches them slip into granite-boulder habitat where their olive-green speckled bodies and buttery-yellow bellies perfectly match the landscape. For Erin Lundy, conservation manager at the Aquarium, the moment a released frog immediately catches a fly on a streamside rock confirms what her team has accomplished: "We've done it. He's functional. He'll be out here forever."

The frogs face relentless pressures—invasive trout species, climate change, habitat loss, and most critically, chytrid fungus, a deadly pathogen ravaging amphibians worldwide. Yet through a coordinated 20-plus-year recovery effort involving San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, multiple zoos, and government agencies, the species survives in human care. Each release represents not just frog survival, but the restoration of ecological complexity: these amphibians connect freshwater and terrestrial ecosystems in ways few other animals do, moving between tadpole and adult life stages.
quick_facts: 650 frogs released into San Gabriel Mountains in August
Fewer than 200 frogs remain in wild southern population
Nearly 400 of released frogs bred at Aquarium of the Pacific
Captive breeding program began as salvage effort after 2003 wildfire
Species once so abundant biologists could barely walk without stepping on them
